item.title: Coherent and ultra-low-power EDSR with a flopping-mode spin qubit in germanium
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Flopping-mode hole spin qubit in planar Ge achieves 99.76% single-qubit gate fidelity (tXπ=88 ns) and T2ϕ,CPMG3=130 μs with −52 dBm drive power.

Grade 0.518 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Alexei Orekhov, Wonjin Jang, Pan Zhang, Konstantinos Tsoukalas, Fabian Oppliger, Franco De Palma, Elena Acinapura, Younghun Ryu, Inga Seidler, Lisa Sommer, Leonardo Massai, Felix J. Schupp, Matthias Mergenthaler, Stefano Bosco, Patrick Harvey-Collard, Pasquale Scarlino

Figure

Single-qubit randomized benchmarking survival probability versus number of Clifford gates, demonstrating gate fidelities up to 99.76% driven with sub-millivolt amplitudes at 5 mT.

Asks

Can flopping-mode hole spin qubits simultaneously achieve strong transverse spin-electric coupling, suppressed charge-noise sensitivity, and long relaxation times at low magnetic fields?

Before

EDSR on planar Ge single-QD qubits required drive powers around −27 dBm (10 mV gate voltage) at low magnetic fields.

But

Measured at |B|=5 mT nearly in-plane magnetic field and dilution refrigerator temperatures (20 mK base); coherent control operates at Zeeman-degeneracy sweet-spots.

Tools

planar strained Ge/SiGe heterostructure · flopping-mode double quantum dot hole qubit · single-hole transistor charge sensor · electric dipole spin resonance (EDSR) · Pauli spin blockade (PSB) readout

Abstract

Hole spin qubits in semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) enable high-fidelity all-electric control, but conventional electric dipole spin resonance (EDSR) can require substantial rf drive power at the low magnetic fields that are favorable for qubit coherence and readout. In planar Ge hole spin qubits, this can reach -27 dBm at the device, posing challenges for scalable architectures due to heating and crosstalk. Here, we demonstrate a flopping-mode (FM) qubit in Ge, where a single spin is delocalized in a double QD, combining first-order protection against charge noise with exceptionally efficient electric driving. By mapping out coherence sweet-spots as a function of magnetic field orientation we achieve T₂^*= 1.4μs, T₂^Hahn= 11.5 μs, T^(φ, CPMG32)₂= 130 μs, and T₁= 226 μs, and a single-qubit gate fidelity of up to 99.76% for a gate time t_(Xπ) = 88 ns. Importantly, these results are obtained at a nearly in-plane magnetic field of 5 mT using only -52 dBm drive power at the device. We further find that qubit relaxation in this regime is consistent with a two-photon Orbach process, providing a route for further optimization. Our results demonstrate that FM-EDSR supports ultra-low-power, high-fidelity single-qubit operations, improvements that could benefit scalable hole-spin-based architectures and hybrid spin-photon interfaces.

item.title: Highly uniform first-electron position in qubit arrays fabricated on dedicated QSOI(R) 300mm commercial platform
item.description:
Worth a look new result — 300mm wafer-scale QSOI platform achieves 69% yield for first-electron charge detection across 546 plunger-gate stability diagrams, with first-electron position dispersion of 21 mV±35 mV over 377 quantum dots.

Grade 0.451 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Silicon quantum electronics” · Johan Pelloux-Prayer, Elise Prin, Giselle A. Elbaz, Pierre-Louis Julliard, Amaryllis Comiti, Clément Nguyen, Sylvain Martin, Patrick Torresani, Renan Lethiecq, Carlos Augusto Suarez Segovia, Franck Arnaud, Etienne Nowak, Tristan Meunier, Bruna Cardoso Paz

Figure

Left: wafer map showing charge-stability diagrams across 91 dies. Right: histogram of the gate voltage corresponding to the first detected electron across 377 quantum dots, centered at 21 mV with a ±35 mV spread.

Asks

Can an adapted commercial 28nm FD-SOI CMOS platform achieve wafer-scale electrostatic uniformity and reproducible few-electron quantum dot operation?

Before

Standard 28nm FD-SOI had room-temperature threshold-voltage dispersion σVTH=385 mV (reduced to 41.1 mV here); matched-pair ΔVTH/2 standard deviation was 59 mV in prior 300mm Si qubit arrays.

But

Tested on a single best-performing wafer split at ∼2 K wafer temperature under DC probing; automated charge detection routine did not dynamically optimize detector sensitivity.

Tools

300mm QSOI quantum platform · cryogenic semi-automatic wafer prober (sub-2K) · charge sensing with single-electron transistors (SET) · TCAD electrostatics simulation

Abstract

We report progress toward the development of a quantum silicon-on-insulator (QSOI(R)) technology compatible with 300mm CMOS fabrication and adapted from the 28nm Fully-Depleted SOI (28nm FD-SOI) platform for scalable quantum computing. We compare quantum devices fabricated with standard 28nm FD-SOI and QSOI(R) technologies, and show striking improvements of room temperature electrostatic properties of the individual device. Moreover, the QSOI(R) technology has significantly reduced the device variability and the dispersion of device properties at the wafer level. Transistor metrics are reproduced by TCAD simulations showing that the electrostatics of the devices behave as expected for QSOI(R) technology. Wafer-scale measurements at sub-2K show reproducible quantum dots down to the few-electron regime with 69% yield for successful charge detection of the first electron and a dispersion of the first electron position of ±35 mV over 377 quantum dots. These results establish QSOI(R) as a promising platform for CMOS-compatible quantum device co-integration.

item.title: Neutral atom quantum computing for materials science and quantum chemistry
item.description:
Long shot review — Neutral atom arrays scale past 103 physical qubits and provide >99.5% two-qubit gate fidelities, enabling continuous-time Hamiltonian simulation, QUBO/MWIS graph optimisation, and transversal logical operations for quantum chemistry and materials science.

Grade 0.421 · 1.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · J. D. Pritchard

Figure

Schematic of a neutral atom computing setup and single-atom fluorescence imaging on a 15×15 optical tweezer array generated via spatial light modulators and acousto-optic deflectors.

Asks

How do neutral atom quantum computing platforms address simulation and optimisation challenges in materials science and quantum chemistry across analogue and digital paradigms?

But

Materials and chemistry applications require utility-scale hardware (105 physical qubits, >106 T-gates), far exceeding current device sizes. Single-species mid-circuit readout causes light scattering and crosstalk.

Tools

optical tweezer arrays · Rydberg dipole blockade · spatial light modulators (SLM) · acousto-optic deflectors (AOD) · dual-species/alkaline-earth atom registers

Abstract

Neutral atom arrays have emerged as versatile platforms for performing both digital and analogue quantum computing and simulation, with demonstrations ranging from large-scale programmable Hamiltonians realising topological phases or weighted graph optimisation to error-corrected logical qubits with transverse gate operations. This paper provides a broad overview to the neutral atom platform, and the potential applications relevant to materials science and quantum chemistry.
